Reliability is a budget conversation, not an uptime aspiration

Reliability is an engineering discipline with a currency: the error budget. SLOs are signed contracts with the business, budgets gate releases without politics, and chaos drills prove recovery paths work before reality tests them. When incidents happen, the response is a rehearsed system — roles, ladders and a decision log.
The practice covers SLO design, alert quality (precision matters more than volume), toil elimination, and the incident-review loop that converts every failure into either a guardrail or a test.
Below: the failure modes that make SRE programs decorative, the reference architecture of budget-gated delivery, and the console that keeps the honest numbers.
Four ways SRE programs become decorative
Every one of these ends with 'the SLO dashboard is green but the customer is angry' — the countermeasures bind budgets to release decisions and alerts to user pain.

widgets.title: Incident lifecycle — click stages for the rehearsal contract

stages.name: Detect
stages.detail: Detection is a burn-rate breach on a journey SLO — pages carry the journey, the burn multiple and the dashboard link; symptom-only alerts were deleted with a ledger entry.

stages.name: Respond
stages.detail: Incident commander, ops lead, comms lead — roles rehearsed in game days; the on-call acts from the runbook, not from memory.

stages.name: Mitigate
stages.detail: Mitigation prefers reversible actions (rollback, feature flag, shed) over heroic fixes; the timeline logs every action with its evidence.

stages.name: Communicate
stages.detail: Customer-impact statements use the same arithmetic as the SLO (affected journeys × duration × volume) — no adjectives without numbers.

stages.name: Learn
stages.detail: Blameless review within a week; remediation items with owners and deadlines verified by drill; repeat classes escalate to the governance backlog.

widgets.note: The lifecycle is rehearsed quarterly in game days — the incident that surprises nobody is the one that costs least.
